inputs.source: On-call engineer's chat request, SSO authenticated

instructions.note: "Do not ask for confirmation; the engineer is busy" removes the only possible safety net (human confirmation) before irreversible production actions purely through instruction text, with no architectural backstop. This is exactly the condition the control_decay model calls dependent-by-design: there is no structural gate to decay, because one was never built.

The agent will deploy 'the named service' or run 'the named migration' on request with no enumerated allowlist of permitted services/migrations, no scoping logic, and no limit on call frequency or session duration described anywhere in the design.

controls.name: Cloud provider audit log of production actions
controls.decay_rationale: Recorded by the cloud platform outside agent or model control, so it does not decay with model capability. However it captures only the action and the engineer's identity, not the original request or the agent's reasoning, so it cannot by itself establish what was asked or why.

controls.name: Chat transcript history
controls.decay_rationale: Not defeated by model capability growth. It is defeated by a permissions gap: the engineer who requested the action can delete their own transcript, erasing the only record of what was actually asked and how the agent interpreted it, for actions already logged under that same engineer's name.

controls.name: Human approval gate before production deploy or migration
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate would not decay with model capability. It is currently absent by explicit instruction ('Do not ask for confirmation'), not by architecture, so there is nothing to decay yet, but also nothing preventing a mistaken or malicious instruction from executing.

controls.name: Immutable log of the original request and agent reasoning, tied to the audit log entry
controls.decay_rationale: Would not decay with model capability if written to the same store as the cloud audit log and not deletable by the acting engineer. Currently missing: the only such record (chat history) is user-deletable and disconnected from the audit log.

findings.title: Irreversible production database migration runs on trusted instruction with no approval gate and no step/runtime bound

attack_path.note: On-call engineer asks the agent to run a named migration.
Agent runs the migration immediately using the engineer's PAT; prompt.md:3 forbids confirmation; no step or runtime limit is declared.

threat_refs.name: Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: A new input channel (ticket system, webhook, CI trigger) begins feeding migration requests to the agent without SSO-equivalent authentication, or a new tool lets the agent pull unreviewed external content into the deployment/migration request context, turning the source from trusted (T) to untrusted (U).

evidence.observation: "run the named migration in production using the engineer's credentials" combined with "Do not ask for confirmation" means the irreversible action executes with zero preventive control.
"Database migrations cannot be rolled back automatically" confirms irreversibility (S3 sink), and no step or runtime limit is described.

recommendations.action: Require a raw_action human approval gate (showing the exact migration script and target environment from the system of record, not a model summary) before any production database migration executes.
Require migration scripts to include a verified rollback/snapshot step, or block execution of migrations that declare no rollback path.

findings.title: Production service deploy runs on trusted instruction with no approval gate

attack_path.note: On-call engineer asks the agent to deploy a named service.
Agent deploys immediately using the engineer's PAT; no confirmation permitted.

forecast.watch_signal: Same as the migration finding: an unauthenticated or lower-trust input channel begins reaching the deploy capability, reclassifying the source from trusted to untrusted.

evidence.observation: "deploy the named service ... using the engineer's credentials" with no confirmation step.

recommendations.action: Require approval or a staged/canary rollout gate for production deploys, at least for services above a defined blast-radius threshold.

findings.title: Shared-identity logging plus deletable transcript defeats non-repudiation for irreversible agent actions

attack_path.note: Engineer instructs deploy or migration via chat.
Irreversible action executes using the engineer's own PAT.
Records only that the engineer's identity performed the action, not what was actually requested or why.
The only record of the actual request and the agent's interpretation of it; the engineer who made the request can delete it.

forecast.watch_signal: The agent gains any ability to modify its own logging configuration, or retention/immutability settings on the cloud audit log are loosened or made owner-configurable, or bulk/automatic transcript deletion is enabled, removing the last independent record alongside the already-deletable transcript.

evidence.observation: "Every production action is recorded in the cloud audit log under the engineer's name" combined with "The only record of what the agent was asked, and why it acted, is the chat transcript. Engineers can delete their own chat history." Together these mean an irreversible production action can be fully attributed to an engineer's identity with no surviving, tamper-proof record of what was actually asked, whether the agent acted correctly on that request, or whether the instruction was even given by that engineer's informed choice.

recommendations.action: Write the full request text and the agent's interpretation/tool-call payload to the same immutable store used for the cloud audit log, with retention the requesting engineer cannot alter, so every S2/S3 action carries a tamper-evident explanation.
Periodically reconcile cloud audit log entries for prod_deploy/db_migrate against surviving transcript records; alert when a transcript tied to an irreversible action is missing or deleted.

rating.rationale: Inherent and residual risk are driven by two S3/S2 sinks (irreversible production database migration; partially-reversible production deploy) reached directly by a trusted, SSO-authenticated source, with the autonomy modifier applied because no step or runtime limit is declared. Residual equals inherent because the only existing controls (cloud audit log, chat transcript) are detective and earn no tier credit under rubric section 5; the one control that would matter, a human approval gate, is explicitly disabled by prompt instruction ('Do not ask for confirmation') rather than merely absent by oversight. The forecast rises to critical under two independent paths: (1) if any future input channel expansion turns the currently trusted-only source into one that can carry untrusted content, the base matrix cell jumps from moderate/low to critical/high; (2) if the agent or its operators ever gain the ability to loosen logging/retention controls, the last independent record of an irreversible action disappears entirely, compounding the existing repudiation gap. The single control whose decay moves the forecast most is the still-missing approval gate: because it was never built, there is no structural control today to credit, and every escalation path leads straight to critical.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design described in prompt.md and the accompanying runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; no actual tool manifest, IaC, or runtime configuration file was provided to verify enforcement.
No MCP, A2A, or formal tool schema was supplied; capabilities were inferred from the narrative description of 'deploy' and 'migrate' actions and scored at medium confidence.

The autonomy level (A3 vs A4) and the applicability of the autonomy modifier were judgment calls, since no explicit reporting/digest mechanism nor explicit step/runtime limits were described; the modifier was applied per the literal rubric condition (both fields null/undeclared).

No untrusted (U) input source was identified in the provided artifacts; the design states only on-call engineers can reach the assistant with no outside content in context. All findings therefore concern trusted-source misuse and accountability failure rather than indirect prompt injection, and should be revisited if that isolation claim changes.
